core_principles.title: Hope and practical preparation
core_principles.description: Hope can sit alongside planning. Invite the person with ALS into decisions, discuss likely needs early and respect their preferences.

core_principles.title: Support should fit the person
core_principles.description: Equipment can improve comfort and reduce effort. Increasing support needs reflect changing health; using an aid does not mean giving up.

core_principles.title: Work with the treating team
core_principles.description: Caregiver observations are valuable. Report changes, ask questions and request specialist input instead of relying on a single number or another family’s treatment settings.

core_principles.title: Oxygen readings do not measure CO₂
core_principles.description: Normal SpO₂ does not rule out under-ventilation. Sleep changes, morning headaches or new breathlessness deserve respiratory assessment.

core_principles.title: Learn from experience without assuming the same outcome
core_principles.description: Community accounts can help with preparation and routines. They cannot guarantee a treatment response, prevent every emergency or predict another person’s progression.

key_principles: Discuss breathing, swallowing and equipment needs early with the treating team.
Respect the person with ALS’s goals, preferences and right to informed decisions.
Normal oxygen saturation does not rule out CO₂ retention or breathing weakness.
A feeding tube can support nutrition but does not eliminate aspiration risk.
Use medicines, oxygen and ventilator settings only according to the individual care plan.
Report sudden changes promptly; do not assume every new symptom is caused by ALS.
Combine practical caregiver experience with clinical assessment and reliable guidance.
Keep trained help, essential supplies, emergency contacts and tested backups ready.

categories.name: Respiratory Care & BiPAP
categories.section_note: Plan breathing support and emergency equipment with the ALS respiratory team before a crisis. The right equipment depends on the person’s assessment; oxygen and manual ventilation need an individual prescription or emergency plan and appropriate training.

questions.question: What is BiPAP?
questions.answer:
BiPAP means bilevel positive airway pressure. It is a form of non-invasive ventilation (NIV), usually delivered through a mask, that supports breathing when respiratory muscles are weak.

Understanding the two pressures
SettingWhat it does
IPAP — inspiratory pressureThe higher pressure during breathing in helps air enter the lungs and reduces the effort needed to take a breath.
EPAP — expiratory pressureThe lower pressure during breathing out helps keep the airway open. It does not actively push carbon dioxide out.
Pressure supportThe difference between IPAP and EPAP assists ventilation. Moving enough air in and out helps clear carbon dioxide (CO₂).
Settings are individual. The respiratory team selects the machine, mask, mode and settings. A CPAP machine provides a single pressure and should not be substituted for prescribed bilevel ventilatory support.

sources.label: NHS: how bilevel ventilation and pressure support work

questions.question: When Does a PALS Need BiPAP, How to Decide?
questions.answer:
Discuss breathing support with the ALS respiratory team when symptoms or breathing tests suggest respiratory muscle weakness. Do not wait for several warning signs or a low oxygen reading before asking for assessment.

Why normal SpO₂ can be misleading

Weaker breathing muscles can reduce the amount of air moved through the lungs. CO₂ may build up, sometimes first during sleep. A pulse oximeter measures oxygen saturation (SpO₂), not CO₂; an apparently normal reading does not rule out under-ventilation.

Changes to report

  • Broken sleep, waking frequently, gasping or unusual restlessness at night.
  • Difficulty lying flat, needing more pillows or sleeping in a recliner.
  • Morning headaches, daytime sleepiness or unusual fatigue.
  • Breathlessness while talking, eating or with usual activities.
  • Faster breathing, a weaker cough, or falling overnight oxygen readings. A fast resting pulse is also worth reporting, but has many possible causes.

What the assessment may include

The team considers symptoms together with respiratory muscle tests, such as FVC/VC, SNIP or MIP, and may arrange overnight monitoring and CO₂ or blood-gas testing.

Use an agreed monitoring plan. There is no universal home oxygen-reading rule for starting BiPAP or supplemental oxygen. Ask the respiratory team what changes should trigger a call for this person.
Seek urgent help: Severe or sudden breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips, new confusion or difficulty waking need immediate medical assessment. Follow the emergency plan and call 112 in India when emergency help is needed.

sources.label: NICE: assessment and management of motor neurone disease
MND Association: support for breathing problems

questions.question: How BiPAP Usage Progresses Over Time? How many hours should PALS use BiPAP daily?
questions.answer:
There is no single daily number of BiPAP hours for everyone with ALS. The respiratory team agrees a schedule and reviews it as symptoms and needs change.

How use may change

  • Initial practice may involve short sessions while awake to get used to the mask and pressure.
  • Many people then use support during sleep; some also need it during naps or daytime activities.
  • Some eventually need prolonged or continuous support. Increasing use should prompt review of ventilation, comfort, skin, secretions and backup arrangements.

When more support is requested

Take the person’s breathlessness seriously and contact the team. New needs can reflect progression, but also mask leaks, discomfort, secretions or illness. Do not ration prescribed support or change pressure settings without guidance.

Using support does not mean failure. Increasing dependence usually reflects changing illness and breathing needs. Continuous NIV alone does not automatically mean that a tracheostomy is required; discuss all options and the person’s wishes.

sources.label: MND Association: support for breathing problems
NICE: assessment and management of motor neurone disease

questions.question: Can early BiPAP help delay tracheostomy?
questions.answer:
Effective NIV can support breathing and quality of life, and some people use it for a long time without tracheostomy. There is no reliable promise that starting BiPAP will delay tracheostomy by a fixed number of months or years.

What helps NIV work well

  • Arrange timely assessment when breathing changes appear.
  • Review mask fit, leaks, comfort and effectiveness with the respiratory team.
  • Use the agreed cough and secretion-management plan.
  • Discuss backup equipment, power, after-hours help and future treatment preferences.
Community experiences vary. Families’ stories can help with practical preparation, but cannot predict another person’s course. NIV supports breathing; it does not stop the underlying disease.

sources.label: NICE: assessment and management of motor neurone disease
MND Association: support for breathing problems

questions.question: When Should we use oxygen concentrator along with BiPAP?
questions.answer:
Supplemental oxygen should be used only under an individual medical prescription. A concentrator supplies oxygen; it does not provide the ventilatory support needed to correct weak breathing.

When a doctor may consider oxygen

Oxygen may be needed for low blood oxygen associated with a chest infection or another lung problem, or for specific goals of care. Clinicians need to assess the cause and monitor CO₂ as appropriate.

What to confirm before home use

  • The prescribed oxygen target, flow, hours and circumstances for use.
  • The compatible connection and equipment setup demonstrated by the respiratory provider.
  • What to do if readings fall, symptoms worsen, power fails or the supply runs out.
Seek urgent help: Do not try to treat new drowsiness or breathing distress by increasing oxygen on your own. Oxygen can worsen CO₂ retention in people with neuromuscular respiratory weakness. Seek help promptly; do not withhold emergency treatment directed by clinicians.

sources.label: MND Association: information for acute and emergency care staff
MND Association: support for breathing problems

questions.question: When Is Tracheostomy Needed? What are the decision criteria?
questions.answer:
Tracheostomy ventilation provides breathing support through a tube in the windpipe. It is a major, personal decision requiring discussion with the specialist team and the person with ALS.

Reasons to review the options

  • Breathing remains inadequate despite an assessment and optimization of NIV.
  • NIV cannot be tolerated or used effectively.
  • Airway protection or secretion clearance becomes very difficult.
  • An acute illness leads to intubation and decisions about ongoing ventilation.

Questions for a planned discussion

  • What benefits, limitations and alternatives apply to this person?
  • What care, training, communication support, staffing and costs would be needed at home?
  • What are the person’s preferences about invasive ventilation, hospital treatment and comfort-focused care?
  • What should happen during an emergency if the person cannot communicate?
There is no automatic threshold. Using NIV all day, one SpO₂ value, or being intubated does not by itself establish that tracheostomy is necessary or the safest option. Decisions depend on clinical assessment and informed preferences.

sources.label: NICE: assessment and management of motor neurone disease
MND Association: support for breathing problems

questions.question: How to delay or avoid emergency tracheostomy?
questions.answer:
Planning ahead can reduce avoidable crises, although it cannot guarantee that an emergency or tracheostomy will be avoided.

Build a practical prevention plan

  1. Arrange regular respiratory reviews and report new breathing or sleep symptoms promptly.
  2. Follow the prescribed NIV and secretion-clearance plan; ask for suction or cough-assist training when indicated.
  3. Review swallowing, nutrition and feeding-tube options before eating becomes a crisis. A tube does not eliminate aspiration risk.
  4. Ask how to recognize infection and whom to contact promptly.
  5. Keep the agreed emergency equipment, power backup, contact numbers and written care preferences accessible. Practise the plan with trained caregivers.
Prepare for the person’s needs. Do not start oxygen, nebulized medicines or manual ventilation just because equipment is available. These require a prescribed plan and appropriate training.

sources.label: NICE: assessment and management of motor neurone disease
MND Association: information for acute and emergency care staff
Hull University Teaching Hospitals: PEG benefits and limitations

questions.question: Why Do Families Delay BiPAP Even After Knowing the Signs?
questions.answer:
Fear, unfamiliar equipment, costs and uncertainty can make starting BiPAP difficult. Families may also worry that accepting support means giving up. These concerns deserve a patient, practical discussion.

Make the decision easier

  • Ask the respiratory team to explain what the symptoms and test results show.
  • Request a mask demonstration and help with a gradual introduction when appropriate.
  • Discuss discomfort, leaks, anxiety, costs and access to support openly.
  • Ask experienced caregivers about daily routines while keeping medical decisions with the treating team.
Hope and preparation can coexist. Normal oxygen readings do not exclude breathing weakness. Report changes and request specialist review rather than waiting for a crisis or trying to decide from the posters alone.

sources.label: NICE: assessment and management of motor neurone disease
MND Association: support for breathing problems

questions.question: What are HME filters and why are they important?
questions.answer:
An HME (heat and moisture exchanger) retains some warmth and moisture from exhaled air and returns it during inhalation. It can help replace the humidifying function of the nose and upper airway when someone has a tracheostomy.

Use the prescribed humidification system

  • The care team chooses an HME or another humidification method according to the circuit, ventilation and secretions.
  • An HME and a bacterial/viral filter do different jobs; some products combine them. Check the exact device.
  • Follow the product and care-team instructions for replacement. Wet, dirty or blocked devices need attention under the care plan.
  • Report thick secretions, difficult suctioning or breathing difficulty; the humidification plan may need review.
Check circuit compatibility. Do not add filters, HMEs or humidifiers to a ventilator circuit without the provider’s guidance.

sources.label: St George’s Hospital: tracheostomy humidification

questions.question: When should we consider a feeding tube (PEG)?
questions.answer:
A gastrostomy tube delivers nutrition, fluid and medicines into the stomach. PEG describes one method of placing it. Discuss the option early so that the person can consider the benefits, risks and alternatives without pressure.

Signs it is time to discuss feeding support

  • Meals take much longer or leave the person exhausted.
  • Swallowing food, drinks or medicines becomes difficult.
  • Coughing or choking during meals, or fear of eating after choking episodes.
  • Ongoing weight loss, reduced intake or difficulty staying hydrated.
  • Repeated chest infections or concern about food or fluid entering the airway.
What planning a feeding tube can help with
ConcernPotential benefit and limitation
Nutrition and hydrationThe tube can supplement intake or become the main route for feeding. A dietitian still needs to review the feed and fluid plan.
Tiring or stressful mealsIt may reduce the amount that must be eaten by mouth. Comfort and preferences still matter.
Timing of the procedureEarly discussion allows assessment of nutrition, breathing and the safest suitable placement method before a crisis.
AspirationTube feeding may reduce risks linked to oral intake, but saliva and refluxed stomach contents can still enter the airway.
Timing is individual. The team assesses respiratory function, procedural risks and the person’s wishes. The specialist team plans the procedure and any breathing support needed during placement.

sources.label: MND Association: swallowing, nutrition and enteral feeding
Hull University Teaching Hospitals: PEG benefits and limitations

questions.question: Can PALS still eat by mouth after PEG?
questions.answer:
Sometimes, depending on the swallowing assessment and the person’s choices. Having a feeding tube does not automatically mean that all eating and drinking by mouth must stop.

What the tube may provide

  • Extra nutrition, hydration or medicines alongside oral intake.
  • Most or all nutrition when oral intake is inadequate or unsafe.
  • Less pressure to finish exhausting meals.

Agree a plan for eating and drinking

The swallowing specialist and dietitian can advise on textures, amounts, positioning and support. Some people choose small tastes for pleasure after discussing the risks; others may be advised to avoid oral intake. Review the plan if coughing, fatigue or swallowing changes.

Aspiration risk remains. A feeding tube does not prevent saliva or reflux from entering the lungs. Mouth care and the prescribed positioning and feeding plan remain important.

sources.label: MND Association: swallowing, nutrition and enteral feeding
MND Association: eating and drinking with acknowledged risk
Hull University Teaching Hospitals: PEG benefits and limitations

questions.question: How to thicken water for PALS with swallowing difficulty (dysphagia)?
questions.answer:
Ask a speech and language/swallowing therapist to assess drinking before starting a thickener. Thickened fluids help some people control a drink, but are not suitable for everyone and do not guarantee prevention of pneumonia.

If a thickener is recommended

  1. Get the exact consistency level and preparation instructions in writing.
  2. Use the recommended medical thickener and product-specific measurements; scoops are not interchangeable between products.
  3. Follow mixing and standing times, and check the texture as taught.
  4. Review hydration, enjoyment, coughing, residue and whether enough fluid is being taken.
Avoid improvised recipes. Do not substitute kitchen xanthan gum or another product without the therapist’s advice. Discuss medicine administration separately with a pharmacist. Worsening intake or swallowing should trigger a review of the overall feeding plan.

sources.label: RCSLT: thickened fluids and swallowing assessment
MND Association: swallowing, nutrition and enteral feeding

questions.question: How can families work with hospital staff during an ALS emergency?
questions.answer:
At home: call and care together

Call 112 immediately in India for severe or worsening breathing difficulty, ineffective ventilation, suspected blocked or displaced tracheostomy, blue/grey colour, collapse or reduced responsiveness. Do not wait for a particular SpO2 reading or try every step first.

One person stays with PALS and provides only trained, prescribed support while another calls emergency services and the treating respiratory/ICU team. If alone, call on speakerphone while staying with PALS.

If external checks and any prescribed, trained suction do not promptly restore effective breathing, stop repeated attempts and obtain urgent skilled help. If the person worsens, escalate immediately. Do not delay help for nebulization or repeated suction cycles.

If a suction catheter will not pass

If the suction catheter will not pass, the TT tube may be blocked or displaced. Call 112 and the respiratory/ICU team now. Do not force the catheter, squeeze an Ambu bag harder, or attempt ventilation through a tube whose patency and position are uncertain.

TT removal/replacement and cuff interventions require a doctor, respiratory therapist or ICU nurse competent and authorized in emergency tracheostomy care. A ventilator technician can help with equipment, but must have specific clinical training and authorization to perform airway procedures. A caregiver should perform an airway intervention only if specifically trained and authorized in that person’s written emergency plan.

Read the emergency escalation guidance.

Bring a concise care summary and explain the person’s usual breathing, communication and feeding needs. Families’ observations can help staff recognize changes quickly.

Information to share

  • The ALS diagnosis, specialist contacts and current medicines.
  • Usual ventilator use and prescribed settings, oxygen prescription if any, and secretion-management needs.
  • How the person communicates, whether they can lie flat, and their swallowing or feeding-tube plan.
  • Their documented care preferences and emergency plan.

If you are concerned

Ask the responsible clinician to explain the plan and, where needed, contact the ALS or respiratory specialist. Mention that oxygen saturation alone may miss CO₂ retention. Seek clarification calmly and promptly; do not independently disconnect or alter treatment.

Plan discharge together. Home care should begin when the clinical team and family have agreed that the required care, equipment, training and support are in place.

questions.question: How Do I Manage Excessive Saliva/Drooling?
questions.answer:
Drooling in ALS usually reflects difficulty swallowing and clearing saliva, rather than increased production. Saliva can pool, irritate skin or enter the airway. Watery saliva, thick secretions and a dry mouth may need different approaches.

Practical care

  • Wiping and skin comfort: keep soft cloths, tissues or absorbent bibs nearby; clean and dry the skin gently.
  • Positioning: ask the care team about supported head elevation or side-lying that is comfortable and compatible with breathing and feeding needs.
  • Oral suction: use a Yankauer or other prescribed oral tip only as trained. Oral suction is different from deep airway or tracheostomy suction.
  • Mouth care: maintain oral hygiene and use the advised mouth-moistening products. Give drinks only if they are safe within the swallowing plan.
  • Hydration: review fluid intake and the feeding plan if saliva becomes sticky.

Food and saliva

Some caregivers notice a thicker or coated mouth feeling after dairy. This does not establish that dairy increases saliva production. Discuss changes with the dietitian so that reducing foods does not reduce needed calories or protein.

When practical care is not enough

Ask about clinician-prescribed medicines such as glycopyrrolate/glycopyrronium or specialist salivary-gland botulinum toxin injections. Benefit and side effects vary.

Watch for thickening. Medicines that reduce drooling may make secretions harder to clear. Report worsening coughing, dry mouth or sticky chest secretions and review the plan.

sources.label: MND Association: saliva problems and practical care
NHS: medicines for drooling and thickened secretions

questions.question: Is glycopyrrolate safe for reducing saliva?
questions.answer:
Glycopyrrolate, also called glycopyrronium, can reduce drooling in some people. It is not suitable or equally helpful for everyone. The prescriber needs to balance saliva reduction against the ability to clear secretions.

Benefits and monitoring
What to look forWhy it matters
Less drooling and improved comfortThese are possible benefits; response varies.
Thicker, stickier secretions or harder airway clearanceReducing watery secretions can make mucus more difficult to clear.
Dry mouth or throat discomfortMouth care and the treatment plan may need adjustment.
Constipation, difficulty passing urine or other new symptomsAnticholinergic side effects need discussion with the prescriber.

Use it with a review plan

  • Confirm the exact product, formulation and prescribed dose with the doctor or pharmacist. Brand names and concentrations can vary.
  • Do not start, stop or change the dose based on another family’s experience.
  • Keep a short record of comfort, drooling, bowel/urine changes and secretion clearance.
  • Discuss alternatives, including specialist botulinum toxin treatment, if benefit is limited or side effects are troublesome.
Seek urgent help: New breathing difficulty or inability to clear secretions needs immediate assessment; do not simply take more saliva-reducing medicine.

sources.label: NHS: medicines for drooling and thickened secretions
NHS: glycopyrronium prescribing and adverse effects

questions.question: How to manage constipation and bowel movements in a bedridden PALS?
questions.answer:
Reduced movement, low fluid intake, changes in food or feeds, and some medicines can contribute to constipation. Look for a change from the person’s usual pattern, hard stools, straining or discomfort. Days without stool alone do not determine severity or which medicine to use.

Build a daily bowel routine

  • Keep a simple record of stool pattern, consistency, discomfort and medicines used.
  • Agree fluid intake with the team, including tube-feed flushes and any kidney or heart-related limits.
  • Include fibre-containing foods or feeds as tolerated and advised; keep regular meal and toileting times.
  • Support gentle movement, repositioning and comfortable toileting where possible.
  • Review medicines with the prescriber when constipation recurs.
When to step up help
SituationPractical next step
A change from usual bowel habits, without alarm symptomsFollow the agreed bowel plan; review fluid intake, diet, routine and comfort.
Persistent constipation, repeated need for rescue treatment or no response to the planContact the clinician or pharmacist. Assessment may identify stool impaction or a medicine-related cause.
Severe pain, repeated vomiting, a swollen abdomen, or inability to pass gasSeek urgent medical assessment. Do not keep adding laxatives or enemas while waiting for advice.

Medicines and fibre supplements

A clinician may recommend macrogol/polyethylene glycol, lactulose or another laxative. Polyethylene glycol is also abbreviated PEG, but is different from a PEG feeding tube. Laxatives can cause cramps, diarrhoea, dehydration or electrolyte changes; no product is guaranteed to be side-effect free.

Products such as Cremaffin have different formulations. Ask about ingredients and suitability, especially with swallowing difficulty or kidney disease. Psyllium/isabgol needs adequate fluid and may be unsuitable with swallowing problems; do not give it dry or put it through a feeding tube without advice. Foods such as prunes or papaya may be included if suitable, but are not a substitute for assessment.

Enemas and suppositories

Use only the product and method advised for this person. Do not assume a homemade plain-water enema is safer, or select treatment from a day-count chart. Rectal treatments can cause harm if used inappropriately.

sources.label: NHS: constipation, self-care and when to seek help
NHS: laxatives, precautions and side effects

questions.question: How to prevent bedsores?
questions.answer:
Pressure sores develop when skin and underlying tissue are damaged by sustained pressure. Limited movement, moisture and poor nutrition can increase risk. A mattress helps, but does not replace a care plan.

Daily prevention

  • Ask a nurse to assess pressure risk and agree a repositioning schedule; the timing should fit the person’s skin, comfort, support surface and medical needs.
  • Use the recommended mattress and cushions, and check powered equipment is working.
  • Inspect pressure areas and skin under masks or other devices regularly. Report persistent colour changes, heat, firmness or pain.
  • Keep skin clean and manage moisture with the advised barrier products. Avoid rubbing or massaging pressure areas.
  • Use trained transfer techniques and suitable equipment to reduce friction. Review nutrition and hydration.
Get help early. Report an open wound or new pressure damage promptly. Do not rely on powder, oil or a water cushion to treat or prevent an injury without professional advice.

sources.label: NICE: pressure ulcer prevention and management

questions.question: Electrolyte Imbalance in PALS - What to Know and How to Manage
questions.answer:
Electrolytes, including sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium, support muscle, heart and brain function. Levels can become too low or too high during illness, dehydration, reduced intake, kidney problems or use of certain medicines. Symptoms alone cannot identify which electrolyte is abnormal.

Changes to report

  • Unusual tiredness or weakness, reduced appetite, nausea or feeling generally unwell.
  • Muscle cramps, spasms, tingling, dizziness or headache.
  • Reduced urine output, significant vomiting or diarrhoea, or difficulty taking usual food and fluids.
Seek urgent help: Confusion, difficulty waking, fainting, seizures, reduced consciousness, palpitations with illness, severe weakness or cold clammy skin need immediate medical assessment. These may also reflect breathing failure, infection or another emergency; do not assume low sodium is the cause.
When blood tests may be needed
SituationWhat to discuss with the treating doctor
Routine follow-upThe interval depends on medicines, kidney function, previous results and current health. There is no universal monthly testing schedule for ALS.
A medicine is started or changedAsk whether and when to recheck electrolytes and kidney function. For example, furosemide monitoring is often arranged after 1–2 weeks, or earlier in higher-risk patients; this is not a rule for every medicine.
Vomiting, diarrhoea, reduced intake or new symptomsContact the team promptly about assessment and tests rather than waiting for the next routine appointment.
Higher riskDiuretics, kidney disease, heart failure or previous abnormalities may require closer monitoring.

What to do safely at home

  • Keep the prescribed feed, fluid and medicine record and share it with the team.
  • Do not add extra salt, potassium, coconut water or supplements to correct a suspected imbalance without medical advice. Too much can also be harmful.
  • ORS may be appropriate for some fluid losses if advised, prepared exactly as directed and compatible with swallowing and fluid restrictions. It is not a treatment for unexplained drowsiness or every electrolyte disorder.
  • Do not give anything by mouth to someone who is difficult to wake or cannot swallow safely.
Results need clinical interpretation. Blood tests guide treatment. Muscle loss is not a reason to accept an abnormal sodium result as a new personal normal, and a sudden change needs assessment.

sources.label: MedlinePlus: fluid and electrolyte balance
MedlinePlus: low blood sodium
NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service: furosemide monitoring

questions.question: What Equipment Do We Need as ALS Progresses?
questions.answer:
Plan equipment around current needs and likely next needs, rather than a rigid early/middle/late-stage list. Breathing, swallowing, mobility and communication can change in different sequences.

Equipment to discuss with the care team
NeedExamples
Movement and personal careWalking aids, wheelchair, hoist, shower chair, grab bars and an accessible toilet setup.
Comfort and skin protectionAdjustable bed, pressure-relieving mattress, suitable seating and bedside table.
CommunicationAlphabet or communication board, accessible call system, communication software or an eye tracker.
Breathing and secretionsPrescribed NIV/ventilator, suction or cough-assist equipment, compatible consumables and training.
Monitoring and continuityThe monitoring devices, power backup and backup equipment specified in the care plan.
Availability and training go together. Confirm the exact model, compatibility, servicing and who will teach caregivers before renting or buying. Oxygen and manual resuscitation equipment require an individual plan; they are not automatic requirements for every person with ALS.

Browse the Home ICU equipment guide and photographs.

sources.label: MND Association: muscle weakness, fatigue and equipment
NICE: assessment and management of motor neurone disease

questions.question: How to Set Up a Home ICU Room for BiPAP + Tracheostomy?
questions.answer:
Begin with a written discharge or home-care plan. NIV through a mask and ventilation through a tracheostomy have different equipment and training needs. The poster is a planning checklist, not a circuit assembly or treatment protocol.

Organize the room by care task
AreaSupplies to confirm with the team
Ventilation and prescribed oxygenThe correct ventilator/BiPAP, circuits, catheter mount, inlet and bacterial filters, and prescribed humidification. HME and Whisper Swivel use depend on the exact circuit. Oxygen concentrator/cylinder and manual resuscitation bag only as specified in the plan.
SuctionSuction machine, suitable oral tip/Yankauer, suction catheters, tubing and machine filter. Saline and 5 ml/10 ml syringes only for the uses demonstrated by the team.
Tracheostomy careThe instructed dressing/cleaning supplies, gauze, gloves, scissors and spare tracheostomy tubes in the specified sizes. Confirm whether antiseptic such as Betadine is appropriate.
NebulizationCompatible nebulizer, T-piece and tubing if prescribed, plus the prescribed medicine or sterile solution. Do not improvise circuit connections.
MonitoringPulse oximeter, blood-pressure monitor and thermometer, or a multiparameter monitor where indicated; agree how to respond to readings and alarms.
Comfort and communicationAdjustable/recliner bed, pressure-relieving mattress, bedside table and accessible communication/call system. TV, Alexa, AC or an air purifier are optional comfort choices.

Room organization

  • Keep supplies labelled, clean, accessible and checked for expiry. Separate clean stock from used items.
  • Keep emergency contacts, care instructions and backup supplies where every trained caregiver can find them.
  • If using CCTV, obtain consent and protect privacy. Remote viewing does not replace a trained caregiver or an alarm-response plan.
  • Arrange professional electrical installation and a tested power plan. Generators must operate outdoors, away from doors, windows and air intakes.

Backups and checks

Confirm spare circuits/filters and tracheostomy supplies, backup ventilation and suction, prescribed oxygen reserve, and feeding supplies with the provider. Check equipment and alarms as instructed. A spare tube does not mean an untrained caregiver should replace it.

View the updated ALSCAS Home ICU setup poster or review power-backup planning.

sources.label: NICE: assessment and management of motor neurone disease
St George’s Hospital: tracheostomy humidification

questions.question: How do I manage if there is a power cut while PALS is on BiPAP or ventilator?
questions.answer:
Follow the person’s written power-failure and emergency plan immediately. A calculator estimate is not a guarantee of safe backup time.

During an outage

  1. Check that the prescribed device has switched to its approved backup supply and is functioning. Respond to alarms as trained.
  2. Contact the caregiver/provider support listed in the plan and arrange transfer early if the available backup will not cover the outage.
  3. If ventilation is interrupted or the person is distressed, call emergency services and use only the backup method you have been trained to provide. Do not delay help while troubleshooting.

Before the next outage

Have the equipment provider and electrician verify the backup arrangement, charging, actual load and tested runtime. Keep emergency contact numbers and the power plan beside the equipment.

Power Backup Calculator & Planning Guide
UPS & Power Backup FAQ

sources.label: NICE: assessment and management of motor neurone disease

questions.question: Will using a power wheelchair or lift make the PALS weaker faster?
questions.answer:
Using a wheelchair, lift or other appropriate aid is not evidence that the person is giving up. Equipment can reduce fatigue, improve transfers and leave more energy for daily activities.

Balance support with suitable movement

  • Ask an occupational therapist or physiotherapist to assess seating, transfers and home access.
  • Use a lift or hoist only with the correct sling and training.
  • Continue individualized movement or range-of-motion exercises where advised; activity should be adapted if it causes pain or excessive fatigue.
  • Review equipment as needs change, including communication access and skin pressure.
Keep expectations realistic. Exercise does not reverse ALS-related nerve damage, and equipment is not proven to slow the underlying disease. The aim is comfort, safety, participation and maintaining useful function where possible.

sources.label: MND Association: muscle weakness, fatigue and equipment
